cards.explanation: The answer is True. The Israelites cry out to the LORD, and the text says why: Jabin had nine hundred chariots of iron, and he had harshly oppressed them for twenty years (Judges 4:3). Jabin is the king of Canaan, by the way. Twenty years of that, and crying out sounds about right to me.

The LORD tells Barak to march to Mount Tabor with ten thousand men. Deborah, the prophetess judging Israel, summons Barak and says the LORD commands him: “Go and march to Mount Tabor, taking with you ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun.” (Judges 4:6) Ten thousand men is a big crowd to herd up a mountain. I can barely get six cookie cutters to line up straight.

The LORD will deliver Sisera into Barak's hand. He says, “And I will draw out Sisera the commander of Jabin’s army, his chariots, and his troops to the River Kishon, and I will deliver him into your hand.” (Judges 4:7) Notice who is doing the delivering, friends. The LORD is the One who draws Sisera out and the One who delivers him.

The answer is False. Barak says, “If you will go with me, I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go.” (Judges 4:8) His answer depends on Deborah coming along. I think he wants some company for the road, and honestly, I get that.

The answer is woman. Deborah says the LORD “…will be selling Sisera into the hand of a woman.” (Judges 4:9) Sisera is the commander of Jabin's army, and the text doesn't name her yet. Keep your eyes open as the story keeps rolling.

The answer is False, Barak doesn't wait. After Deborah says “Arise,” the text says, “So Barak came down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men following him.” (Judges 4:14) She asks him, “Has not the LORD gone before you?” I think that question gets a man moving. It would get me out of the kitchen too.
The answer is True. Sisera “…abandoned his chariot and fled on foot.” (Judges 4:15) He commands nine hundred iron chariots, and he leaves with his own two feet. I hope he stretched first, friends.

The reason the text gives is that there was peace between Jabin and Heber. Sisera fled to the tent of Jael, Heber the Kenite's wife, “…because there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.” (Judges 4:17) Sisera is Jabin's army commander. I think he figured a friendly house was a safe place to land.

Sisera wants Jael to tell them no. He says, “Stand at the entrance to the tent, and if anyone comes and asks you, ‘Is there a man here?’ say, ‘No.’” (Judges 4:20) He is the army commander, and I bet he wants to stay hidden. So he's asking Jael to answer no if someone asks whether a man is there.

Jael tells Barak she'll show him the man he's seeking. She says, “Come, and I will show you the man you are seeking.” (Judges 4:22) Then he goes in, and Sisera lies dead with a tent peg through his temple. I think this part is heavy, so I'll just point back to what Deborah told Barak: the LORD would be selling Sisera into the hand of a woman (Judges 4:9).

The answer is False. The kings and princes are called to listen, and then the singer says, “I will sing to the LORD; I will sing praise to the LORD, the God of Israel.” (Judges 5:3) So the praise goes to the LORD, not to the people in the front row. I'd call that a very good use of a microphone.

The earth trembles and the mountains quake. When the LORD marched from the land of Edom, “…the earth trembled, the heavens poured out rain, and the clouds poured down water.” (Judges 5:4) Then, “The mountains quaked before the LORD, the One of Sinai, before the LORD, the God of Israel.” (Judges 5:5) Even the mountains pay attention when He moves.

The answer is new gods. The song says, “When they chose new gods, then war came to their gates.” (Judges 5:8) It puts those two things side by side, and that's the song's own sorrowful look back. I think it's a sober line, and it's a good reminder to keep our hearts with the LORD.

The answer is False. The singers at the watering places “…recount the righteous acts of the LORD, the righteous deeds of His villagers in Israel.” (Judges 5:11) Sisera, Jabin's army commander, doesn't get a mention there. I think a well is a fine place to tell the good stuff.

The answer is great indecision. The song says it twice: “In the clans of Reuben there was great indecision.” (Judges 5:15, 16) Reuben is one of Israel's tribes. We've all stared at two options so long that the moment passed. I think that's the human side of the line.

The answer is True. The song says, “Zebulun was a people who risked their lives; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the battlefield.” (Judges 5:18) Those are the two tribes Barak summoned (Judges 4:10). After a list of tribes who stayed back, that's a real shout-out.

The stars from their courses fought against Sisera. The song says, “From the heavens the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera.” (Judges 5:20) Sisera is Jabin's army commander. The song doesn't explain how the stars fought, so I won't either.

The reason the song gives is that they didn't come to help the LORD. The angel of the LORD says, “Curse Meroz,” and then, “for they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty.” (Judges 5:23) The text says nothing more about Meroz. It's a serious line, so I'll leave it right there.

It's Sisera's mother at that window. The song says, “Sisera’s mother looked through the window; she peered through the lattice and lamented: ‘Why is his chariot so long in coming?’” (Judges 5:28) Sisera is Jabin's army commander. I think this moment is heavy, so I'll let the song's words stand.

She tells herself they're dividing up the spoil. She keeps telling herself, “Are they not finding and dividing the spoil…” (Judges 5:30) That's what she keeps telling herself, right after her wisest ladies answer. This part is heavy, and the song lets it speak for itself.
